headerTitle: MGT705 — Advanced Cost and Management Accounting
subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)

subjective.question: Why is the book value of the equipment considered irrelevant for making equipment replacement decisions?
subjective.answer: The book value of the old equipment is the amount at which it is recorded in the books, i.e. its original cost less accumulated depreciation. It is based on a past (historical) cost that has already been incurred, so it is a sunk cost. A replacement decision affects only future cash flows: the purchase price of the new equipment, its running costs and savings, its disposal value, and the disposal proceeds of the old equipment. Since the book value will not change whichever decision is taken, it is irrelevant for the replacement decision. (Only the disposal value of the old equipment is relevant, because it is a future cash inflow.)

subjective.question: Differentiate between sunk cost and opportunity cost with the help of examples.
subjective.answer: A sunk cost is a past cost that has already been incurred and cannot be changed by any future decision, e.g. a down payment already made for a machine. It is always irrelevant for decision making. An opportunity cost is the benefit foregone by choosing one alternative instead of the next best alternative; it is a future, expected cost and is relevant for decision making. Example: if a factory can be sublet to a friend, the rent foregone when the factory is used for own production is an opportunity cost, whereas money already spent (down payment) is a sunk cost.

subjective.question: Why is direct labor cost treated as a relevant cost in decision making, while fixed costs are treated as irrelevant?
subjective.answer: Direct labor cost changes with the level of production: when more units are produced, more labor is employed and the total labor cost rises, and when production falls, it decreases. It is therefore affected by the decision and is a relevant cost, in both the short term and the long term. For example, if direct labor cost is Rs. 150 per unit, producing 100 units costs Rs. 15,000 while producing 150 units costs Rs. 22,500, so the decision changes the cost. Fixed costs, such as the rent of the building, remain the same in total whatever the level of production, so they are not affected by the decision and are irrelevant for decision making.

subjective.question: What are the non-monetary factors that should be considered in decision making?
subjective.answer: Non-monetary (qualitative) factors are the factors that cannot be measured in money terms but can decide whether a project or order should be accepted. The important ones are: (i) Is there sufficient spare capacity to undertake the project? (ii) Is the overseas customer credit-worthy? (iii) Does the workforce have the necessary skills to undertake the project? (iv) Is the contract likely to result in repeat business with the customer?

subjective.question: Explain the Activity Based Costing (ABC) system.
subjective.answer: Activity Based Costing (ABC) is a costing system in which overheads are assigned to major activities rather than to departments. Costs are accumulated in activity cost pools, and a cost driver is identified for each activity (e.g. number of purchase orders for purchasing, number of production runs for scheduling). The cost of each activity is then charged to products according to the amount of the activity they consume. ABC therefore measures the indirect relevant costs of products more accurately than a traditional system, which absorbs overheads on a single basis such as direct labor hours and treats batch-related expenses as fixed costs.

subjective.question: Explain unit level activities in the ABC system.
subjective.answer: Unit-level activities are activities that are performed every time a unit of a product is produced. They consume resources in proportion to the number of units manufactured, e.g. direct materials, direct labor and energy consumed in machining each unit. The expenses of unit-level activities (direct material cost, direct labor cost and energy cost) vary directly with the number of units produced, unlike batch-level activities, whose cost depends on the number of batches rather than the number of units.

subjective.question: An accountant manager selected the wrong level of hierarchy while assigning costs in an ABC system. Explain the levels of the ABC cost hierarchy and why costs must be assigned at the correct level.
subjective.answer: In ABC, costs are categorized according to their hierarchical levels, and each cost must be assigned at the correct level of the hierarchy: (i) Unit level: costs driven by the number of units produced (direct materials, direct labor, energy). (ii) Batch level: costs driven by the number of batches (setups, purchasing, receiving, inspection, production scheduling). (iii) Product level (product-sustaining): costs that support a whole product line (product design, product testing). (iv) Facility/business level: costs that sustain the whole organization (rent, management salaries). If a cost is analyzed at the wrong level, e.g. a batch-level cost is spread over units as if it were a unit-level cost, the resulting product costs are distorted and decisions taken on them (pricing, product mix) will be wrong. The correct level is the one whose activity actually causes the cost to be incurred.

subjective.question: Case Study: A small but complex manufacturing concern and a well-established commercial bank are both facing costing problems with their conventional costing systems. The bank intends to install an Activity Based Costing (ABC) system, but the manufacturing concern fears to adopt it because of its complexity. As a management consultant, answer the following: 1. What comparative benefits can the manufacturing concern reap using the ABC system? 2. Why should the bank adopt the ABC system? 3. What are the possible disadvantages (any two) of conventional costing faced by the manufacturing concern? 4. Does ABC really suit service-oriented concerns?
subjective.answer: 1. Benefits of ABC for the manufacturing concern: greater costing accuracy; more accurate costing of products, distribution channels and customers; better understanding of overheads; it utilizes unit cost rather than only total cost; it makes waste and non-value-added activities visible earlier; it integrates well with continuous improvement programs; it can facilitate benchmarking; and it eliminates the allocation of irrelevant costs to products. 2. The bank should adopt ABC because ABC can be applied to all overhead costs, not only production overheads, and it can be used just as easily in service costing as in product costing, so the bank can derive realistic costs of its financial products and services. 3. Disadvantages of conventional costing (any two): (i) it may ignore the other cost drivers that contribute to the cost, absorbing all overheads on one arbitrary basis; (ii) it can lead to bad management decisions because it excludes certain non-manufacturing costs; (iii) it is outdated for modern computerized production. 4. Yes, ABC really suits service-oriented concerns. It is as important for the service sector as for manufacturing; hospitals, financial services firms and retailers use ABC because it applies to all overhead costs, not only production overheads.

subjective.question: What is the relationship between Activity Based Budgeting (ABB) and Activity Based Costing (ABC)?
subjective.answer: Activity Based Budgeting (ABB) is the application of ABC principles to the budgeting process. ABC first identifies the activities of the organization and their cost drivers and calculates a cost driver rate for each activity. ABB then uses these activity and cost driver relationships to prepare the budget: the budgeted demand for each product or service is translated into the budgeted quantity of each activity, and the budgeted cost is obtained by applying the cost driver rates. Thus ABC provides the cost information (activities, drivers and rates) on which ABB builds the budget; ABB is simply ABC applied forward to planning instead of backward to costing.

subjective.question: A company is introducing a new mosquito repellent product named "GO MOSQUITO". Being a new product in the market, what phases will it have to go through? Explain the product life cycle and relate it to this product.
subjective.answer: The product life cycle consists of four stages: (i) Introductory: the product is launched; awareness and acceptance are minimal and sales are low. (ii) Growth: sales begin to expand because of introductory promotions and increasing acceptance. (iii) Maturity: sales taper off as new customers are exhausted; sales volume is at its peak but growth stops. (iv) Decline: sales diminish as the product is replaced by new and better versions. For a new mosquito repellent such as "GO MOSQUITO", the product will first pass through the introductory stage (heavy promotion to create awareness), then growth as households start buying it regularly, then maturity when almost all potential customers are using it and competition is strongest, and finally decline when better repellents replace it. Pricing, promotion and costing decisions differ at each stage, e.g. penetration pricing and heavy advertising at introduction, and cost control at maturity.

subjective.question: Suppose you are the management of Q-Mobile Company. They are about to introduce a new mobile with the features of high-priced mobiles for people with low income. Which pricing policy will you suggest for the pricing of the new mobile?
subjective.answer: Q-Mobile is offering the features of high-priced mobiles to low-income customers, so the suggested policy is price penetration. A penetration pricing policy means charging a low price initially in order to gain rapid acceptance of the product and a large market share. It is appropriate here because the target customers have low incomes and are price-sensitive, and because close substitutes (other low-priced mobiles) are available in the market. A high (skimming) price would fail, because low-income buyers cannot pay it and competitors offer similar features.

subjective.question: A scenario of a textile company was given. State the limitations of the cost-plus pricing method and justify with examples.
subjective.answer: (i) The cost-plus price is based on estimated cost, but the selling price itself determines the sales volume, and the sales volume determines the unit cost (because fixed overhead per unit falls as volume rises). This circularity makes the price unreliable. (ii) It ignores demand: customers and market conditions, not cost, decide what price can actually be charged. (iii) It ignores competition and the prices of close substitutes. (iv) Budgeted volume used for overhead absorption may not be achieved, so the price may recover too much or too little overhead. (v) It provides no incentive to control costs, since any cost increase can simply be passed on to the customer as a higher price. (vi) It may price the product out of the market (if costs are high) or leave profit unearned (if the market could bear a higher price). A textile company using cost-plus pricing, for example, may lose export orders to cheaper competitors even though its price is only its own cost plus a fixed markup.

subjective.question: Differentiate between price skimming and price penetration policies with examples.
subjective.answer: Price skimming policy: a high price is charged for a new product when there is no competitor in the market, e.g. Apple iPhone, which has the highest price among mobile phones with no direct competitor for its features. It is suitable only while close substitutes are not available. Price penetration policy: a low price is charged to enter the market quickly where many competitors exist, e.g. China mobiles and tablet PCs, which are sold at low prices in a highly competitive market.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the conventional and alternative approaches to budgeting.
subjective.answer: In the conventional approach, a budget is prepared for a fixed period, normally twelve months, and is usually based on the previous period's figures with incremental adjustments; once set, it is not revised during the year even if conditions change. In the alternative (rolling/continuous) approach, the budget is continuously updated: as each month or quarter passes, a new month or quarter is added at the end, so the budget always covers the next twelve months. The alternative approach keeps the budget realistic and responsive to changing conditions, but it requires more time and effort to prepare and revise repeatedly, whereas the conventional approach is simpler but can become outdated and irrelevant for control.

subjective.question: Differentiate between traditional budgeting and zero-based budgeting.
subjective.answer: Traditional budgeting is incremental: last year's budget is taken as the base and adjusted for inflation and known changes, so past inefficiencies are carried forward automatically. In zero-based budgeting (ZBB), every expense must be justified from zero each period; no expense is accepted merely because it was incurred last year. Managers prepare decision packages for each activity, which are ranked in order of priority. ZBB is mainly used for discretionary expenses such as advertising, research and staff activities, and it helps to eliminate wasteful expenditure, although it is more time-consuming and costly to operate than traditional budgeting.

subjective.question: State the steps for preparation of a sales budget.
subjective.answer: The sales budget is the starting point of the master budget. Its main steps are: 1. Analyze past sales trends and the current market situation. 2. Collect sales estimates from salespersons and regional managers for each territory and product. 3. Estimate the effect of external factors: competition, economic conditions, seasonality and government policy. 4. Decide the selling prices for the budget period. 5. Estimate sales in units for each product, territory and period (month/quarter). 6. Multiply budgeted units by selling prices to obtain budgeted sales revenue. 7. Get the estimates reviewed and approved by top management. 8. Consolidate the product/territory estimates into the total sales budget. 9. Communicate the approved sales budget to production and other departments so that production, purchase and cash budgets can be prepared. 10. Compare actual sales with the budget during the period and revise if conditions change significantly.

subjective.question: Explain the conflicting rules (roles) of budgeting.
subjective.answer: A budget performs several functions, and the requirements of these functions can conflict with each other. The main functions are: planning (quantifying the plan of action), communication and coordination of plans, motivation of managers, and control of activities (comparison of actual results with the budget). The conflict arises because one budget figure cannot serve all purposes equally well: a challenging target may motivate managers but will be a poor planning forecast; a realistic forecast is good for planning but may not motivate; and managers may bias their estimates (budgetary slack) to make control targets easy to achieve. These are the conflicting rules/roles of budgeting that management must balance.

subjective.question: State the functions of a budget and the components of the master budget.
subjective.answer: A budget performs the following functions: (i) Communication of plans: it communicates management's plans to all departments in quantified form. (ii) Motivation of managers: participation in setting targets motivates managers to achieve them. (iii) Control of activities: actual results are compared with the budget and corrective action is taken on variances. The master budget, which summarizes all the individual budgets, consists of a budgeted profit and loss account, a budgeted balance sheet and a cash flow statement (cash budget), expressed in terms of cash inflows and outflows, sales revenues and expenses.

subjective.question: List and briefly explain the stages of the planning process.
subjective.answer: Stage 1 - Establishing objectives: deciding the long-term objectives of the organization. Stage 2 - Identifying potential strategies: searching for courses of action that might lead to the objectives. Stage 3 - Evaluation of strategic options: examining the feasibility and suitability of each option. Stage 4 - Selecting the course of action: choosing the strategy to be followed. Stage 5 - Implementation of long-term plans: converting the strategy into detailed short-term budgets and plans. Stages 6 and 7 - Monitoring actual outcomes and responding to divergences: comparing actual performance with the plan and taking corrective action.

subjective.question: Define contribution margin and state how it is calculated.
subjective.answer: Contribution margin is the difference between sales revenue and variable cost. It is the amount contributed towards covering fixed costs and earning profit. Contribution margin = Sales revenue - Variable costs Contribution margin per unit = Selling price per unit - Variable cost per unit Once fixed costs are covered, the whole contribution margin becomes profit; this is why contribution margin is the key figure in break-even and cost-volume-profit analysis.

subjective.question: From the following data, calculate (a) prime cost and (b) conversion cost: Direct material consumed Rs. 180,000; Direct labor Rs. 120,000; Direct expenses Rs. 20,000; Factory overheads Rs. 90,000.
subjective.answer: Prime cost = Direct material consumed + Direct labor + Direct expenses = Rs. 180,000 + Rs. 120,000 + Rs. 20,000 = Rs. 320,000 Conversion cost = Direct labor + Direct expenses + Factory (production) overheads = Rs. 120,000 + Rs. 20,000 + Rs. 90,000 = Rs. 230,000 (Conversion cost is the cost of converting raw material into finished goods, i.e. all production costs except direct material.)

subjective.question: A company sells a product at Rs. 50 per unit. The variable cost is Rs. 30 per unit and sales are 10,000 units. Direct fixed costs are Rs. 80,000 and common fixed costs are Rs. 50,000. Calculate (a) unit selling price, unit variable cost and unit contribution, (b) total sales revenue, and (c) contribution to direct and common fixed costs.
subjective.answer: Unit contribution = Unit selling price - Unit variable cost = Rs. 50 - Rs. 30 = Rs. 20 per unit Total sales revenue = 10,000 units x Rs. 50 = Rs. 500,000 Total contribution = 10,000 units x Rs. 20 = Rs. 200,000 Contribution after direct fixed costs = Rs. 200,000 - Rs. 80,000 = Rs. 120,000 Profit after common fixed costs = Rs. 120,000 - Rs. 50,000 = Rs. 70,000

subjective.question: Prepare a budgeted income statement from the following data: budgeted sales 50,000 units at Rs. 20 per unit; variable cost Rs. 12 per unit; fixed costs Rs. 250,000.
subjective.answer: Budgeted Income Statement Sales revenue (50,000 units x Rs. 20) = Rs. 1,000,000 Less: Variable costs (50,000 units x Rs. 12) = Rs. 600,000 Contribution = Rs. 400,000 Less: Fixed costs = Rs. 250,000 Budgeted profit = Rs. 150,000

subjective.question: A product is sold at Rs. 100 per unit with a variable cost of Rs. 60 per unit. Current sales volume is 10,000 units and fixed costs are Rs. 250,000. Management proposes reducing the selling price by 10%, which is estimated to increase sales volume by 30%. Evaluate the proposal.
subjective.answer: Current position: Unit contribution = Rs. 100 - Rs. 60 = Rs. 40. Total contribution = 10,000 x Rs. 40 = Rs. 400,000. Profit = Rs. 400,000 - Rs. 250,000 = Rs. 150,000. Proposed position: New selling price = Rs. 100 - 10% = Rs. 90. New volume = 10,000 + 30% = 13,000 units. Unit contribution = Rs. 90 - Rs. 60 = Rs. 30. Total contribution = 13,000 x Rs. 30 = Rs. 390,000. Profit = Rs. 390,000 - Rs. 250,000 = Rs. 140,000. The total contribution falls by Rs. 10,000 (from Rs. 400,000 to Rs. 390,000), so the price reduction should NOT be made; the 30% increase in volume is not enough to compensate for the lower contribution per unit.

subjective.question: A company normally sells its product at Rs. 11 per unit. It has spare capacity and receives an offer for an extra 1,000 units at Rs. 8 per unit. The variable cost is Rs. 6 per unit and there will be no increase in fixed costs. Should the company accept the order or not?
subjective.answer: Relevant cost per unit of the extra order = variable cost only = Rs. 6 (fixed costs will be incurred anyway because spare capacity exists, so they are irrelevant). Extra contribution = (Rs. 8 - Rs. 6) x 1,000 units = Rs. 2,000. Since the special price of Rs. 8 is above the relevant (variable) cost of Rs. 6 and the company has spare capacity, the order adds Rs. 2,000 to profit and should be ACCEPTED, provided non-monetary factors are favorable (e.g. the order does not disturb the existing market price of Rs. 11 and the customer is credit-worthy).

subjective.question: Fixed costs of a company are Rs. 200,000 and its contribution margin ratio is 40%. Budgeted sales are Rs. 800,000. Using the margin of safety formula, calculate the margin of safety in rupees and as a percentage.
subjective.answer: Break-even sales = Fixed costs / Contribution margin ratio = Rs. 200,000 / 40% = Rs. 500,000 Margin of safety = Actual (budgeted) sales - Break-even sales = Rs. 800,000 - Rs. 500,000 = Rs. 300,000 Margin of safety ratio = Rs. 300,000 / Rs. 800,000 x 100 = 37.5% Sales can fall by Rs. 300,000 (37.5%) before the company starts making a loss.

subjective.question: What is supply chain management? State its five basic components.
subjective.answer: Supply chain management (SCM) is the combination of art and science that goes into improving the way a company finds the raw components it needs to make a product or service and delivers it to customers. Its five basic components are: 1. Plan: developing a strategy for managing all the resources that go toward meeting customer demand. 2. Source: choosing suppliers and managing the procurement of goods and services. 3. Make: scheduling and managing the production process. 4. Deliver: coordinating receipt of orders, warehousing and transportation to customers (logistics). 5. Return: handling defective products returned by customers and providing after-sales support.

subjective.question: Is a unit level cost activity plan helpful for a new organization? Justify your answer.
subjective.answer: Yes. Unit-level activities are those performed for every unit produced, and their costs (direct materials, direct labor, energy) can be measured per unit from the very beginning. For a new organization, planning costs at unit level is helpful because: it establishes the basic variable cost of each product, which is needed for pricing and break-even decisions; it identifies which resources are consumed by each unit, so wastage can be controlled; and it provides the foundation on which batch-level, product-level and facility-level costs are later built as the organization grows. Without unit-level cost information, a new organization cannot know whether its products are profitable at all.

subjective.question: Explain the stages of target costing as a cost management tool.
subjective.answer: In target costing, the selling price is determined first, from marketing factors and customer research, i.e. the price customers will be prepared to pay. The stages are: Stage 1: Determine the target price which customers will be prepared to pay for the product. Stage 2: Deduct a target profit margin to determine the target cost. Stage 3: Estimate the actual cost of the product. Stage 4: If the estimated actual cost exceeds the target cost, investigate ways of driving down the actual cost (e.g. value engineering) until the target cost is achieved.
